en: The Jātaka:
The Ninth Chapter, The Section on Vultures (Gijjhavagga)
3. The Mahāsuvajātaka:
“When a tree has come into fruition, the birds fly down and eat of it.”
Knowing that the tree’s fruit has perished, the birds fly away from there in every direction.
Wander on your journey, O red-beaked one; do not die!
"Why do you, O bird, brood upon a withered tree?
Tell me this, you who resemble springtime:
why, O bird, do you not abandon the withered tree?"
“Those indeed who become a support for their friends,
O swan, in times of death, in suffering, or in happiness—
whether they have reached their end or not— they do not abandon them.”
The noble ones, recollecting the Dhamma of the noble ones:
"I am one among those noble ones, O swan;
this tree is my kinsman and my friend."
"One who seeks a livelihood cannot bear to abandon that;
for knowing it to be exhausted, this is not the Dhamma.
"Excellent! A witness has been provided."
Familiarity breeds intimacy;
if you find this Dhamma pleasing,
you will be praised by those who possess true knowledge.
Therefore, O bird that flies on wings, I grant you a boon;
choose a boon, O Vakkaṅga.
“Whatever you desire in your mind.
“If your honor would grant me a boon, O swan,
let this tree regain its life.”
“Thus it has branches and bears fruit, well-grown;
let the honey-seeker stand by it, shining forth.
“Behold that noble, fruit-bearing tree, my friend!”
May you have companionship with the udumbara tree;
may it grow up with branches and fruit,
standing beautiful for one who desires its honey.
“Thus, Sakka, may you be happy together with all your kinsmen,
just as I am happy today.”
"Having seen the tree bearing fruit,
and having granted a boon to Suvassa,
he made the tree fruitful."
He set out together with his wife for the Nandana grove of the gods.
Thus ends the third Jātaka, the Mahāsuvajātaka.
